title: Hamdanid Emirates
capsule: The Hamdanid dynasty was a Shia Arab dynasty of the Banu Taghlib tribe that ruled two separate emirates: the Emirate of Mosul (905–979) in northern Mesopotamia, founded by Hamdan ibn Hamdun, and the Emirate of Aleppo (944–1004) in northern Syria. Sayf al-Dawla (r. 944–967), ruler of Aleppo, was the dynasty's most celebrated figure, conducting some forty campaigns against the Byzantines along the Taurus frontier and patronizing the great Arab poet al-Mutanabbi at his court. After Sayf al-Dawla's death, Byzantine pressure intensified and the Fatimid Caliphate absorbed the Aleppo emirate in 1016; the Mosul branch had already been extinguished by the Buyids in 979.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The two Hamdanid emirate territories are attested through Arabic chronicles (Miskawayh, Ibn al-Athir) and Byzantine sources; the Mosul and Aleppo cores are well documented, but the extent of seasonal or nominal suzerainty in the surrounding steppe and Jazira is uncertain.
